summary: This is a markdown specification for a code review agent that automatically audits Bash scripts in a project against best practices. The agent reads shell files, checks for safety patterns like proper error handling headers and grep safeguards, reports violations with file locations, but never modifies any code—it's read-only analysis only.

explanations.10: The agent references an external 'bash-best-practices' skill document that contains the actual rules being checked; this specification just describes how the agent applies those rules.
explanations.13: Projects can define their own additional Bash rules (like specific ways to handle exit codes or load scripts) that should also be checked if they exist in the project.
explanations.18: Running the checks in an isolated agent keeps the many shell file details from cluttering the main conversation context; only the findings get reported back.
explanations.33: This example command finds all .sh files and searches each one for the critical safety directive; if it's missing, the file is flagged.
explanations.36: When grep is used in a pipeline with set -euo pipefail active, a grep that finds nothing exits with code 1, which would crash the script—so '|| true' must follow to prevent that.
explanations.38: Long blocks of text (like help messages or templates) defined inline as heredocs make scripts hard to read and maintain; they should live in separate template files instead.
explanations.40: The default soft limit is around 300 lines per script; anything longer should be considered for splitting into smaller functions, though this isn't a hard error.
explanations.45: Some projects define their own strict rules about how scripts should behave (like always returning specific exit codes or following a loader pattern); those custom rules should be checked too if the project has them.
